articles.title: CEO da OpenAI muda nome para ‘Ram Altman’ no X após polêmica sobre memória de computadores | G1
articles.standfirst: Sam Altman afirmou que computadores pessoais aproveitam pouco a memória disponível. Após repercussão negativa, disse que sua declaração foi tirada de contexto.
articles.summary: Sam Altman afirmou que computadores pessoais aproveitam pouco a memória disponível. Após repercussão negativa, disse que sua declaração foi tirada de contexto.
articles.body:
O CEO da OpenAI , Sam Altman, mudou seu nome para "Ram Altman" na rede social X após ser criticado por declarações sobre o uso de memória RAM.

Em entrevista ao podcast Cheeky Pint, em 29 de outubro, ele afirmou que o componente seria mais bem aproveitado em data centers do que em computadores pessoais.

Segundo Altman, diante da oferta limitada, seria mais eficiente concentrar a memória nessas instalações, utilizadas por empresas para processar informações e operar sistemas de IA.

O executivo argumentou que os computadores pessoais passam boa parte do tempo sem utilizar toda a memória disponível, enquanto os equipamentos desses centros podem aproveitá-la de forma mais eficiente.

"Do ponto de vista da distribuição global, é péssimo que todos tenham uma boa parte da oferta limitada de DRAM do mundo armazenada em seus próprios computadores, sendo usada apenas 5% do tempo", afirmou.

O CEO da OpenAI, Sam Altman, discursa no Conselho de Segurança das Nações Unidas durante uma sessão sobre inteligência artificial, na sede da ONU — Foto: Reuters

Altman acrescentou que, em um cenário de escassez, o ideal seria aproveitar ao máximo a memória disponível em servidores na nuvem, em vez de distribuí-la entre computadores domésticos.

A declaração provocou críticas nas redes sociais, especialmente entre usuários que defendem a possibilidade de executar sistemas de IA diretamente em seus computadores, sem depender dos serviços de grandes empresas.

Também chamada de memória de acesso aleatório (RAM, na sigla em inglês), essa tecnologia armazena temporariamente os dados que computadores e celulares utilizam durante seu funcionamento.

Ao abrir um jogo ou aplicativo, por exemplo, parte das informações necessárias para executá-lo fica armazenada na RAM. Quando o aparelho é desligado, esses dados são apagados. Por isso, ela é conhecida como uma espécie de memória de curto prazo.

Sua capacidade é medida em gigabytes (GB). Em geral, quanto maior a quantidade de RAM disponível, mais tarefas um dispositivo consegue executar ao mesmo tempo. O desempenho, porém, também depende de outros componentes.

Já a DRAM, mencionada por Altman, é um tipo de memória RAM amplamente utilizado em computadores, celulares e outros aparelhos eletrônicos.

O avanço da inteligência artificial tem aumentado a procura por esses componentes, especialmente por aqueles utilizados em grandes centros de processamento de dados.

Empresas de tecnologia estão investindo bilhões de dólares na construção de data centers e na compra de equipamentos capazes de executar sistemas de IA cada vez mais avançados.

A discussão envolve duas formas de utilizar a inteligência artificial:

Computação em nuvem: os programas funcionam em servidores de empresas, como a OpenAI. Nesse modelo, o usuário acessa a tecnologia pela internet, sem precisar de um computador tão potente.

IA local: os sistemas funcionam diretamente no computador do usuário, utilizando a memória e a capacidade de processamento do próprio aparelho.

A principal diferença é que a IA local permite executar determinados modelos sem depender constantemente de uma conexão com a internet ou de servidores externos.

Para isso, porém, é necessário ter equipamentos com capacidade suficiente para executar os programas.

Parte dos usuários interpretou a fala de Altman como uma defesa da concentração dos recursos de computação em big techs, em vez de disponibilizá-los para computadores pessoais.

A declaração também levantou discussões sobre o futuro do acesso à inteligência artificial e o risco de os consumidores dependerem cada vez mais de serviços pagos na nuvem.

Após a repercussão negativa, Altman afirmou no X que suas declarações foram tiradas de contexto e que não é contrário ao uso de memória RAM em computadores pessoais.

"Eu realmente quero que o mundo tenha toneladas de memória e que as pessoas coloquem o quanto quiserem em seus computadores. É uma droga que isso tenha sido tirado de contexto", escreveu.

O executivo também disse que defende há muito tempo o aumento da produção mundial de memória.

Segundo Altman, sua declaração se referia ao uso mais eficiente desses componentes em um momento de oferta limitada, e não a uma oposição permanente à utilização de memória RAM em computadores domésticos.

Também defendeu ampliar a produção para atender tanto às empresas de tecnologia quanto aos consumidores.

articles.title: EU rules on Artificial Intelligence devices will apply in NI
articles.summary: Some EU rules on Artificial Intelligence will apply in Northern Ireland, the UK government says.
articles.body:
Some EU rules on Artificial Intelligence (AI) will apply in Northern Ireland, the UK government has said.

However the regulation of AI in NI will largely be a matter for the UK government and Stormont.

EU rules will only apply to physical goods which have an embedded AI system.

They will apply due to the Windsor Framework, the Brexit deal which keeps NI inside the EU's single market for goods.

The EU's AI Act was passed in 2024 and in 2025 the European Commission proposed that the parts concerning goods should apply in NI. That has been under negotiation with the UK since then.

The government said: "The EU AI Act does not apply to NI in full. It applies only where an AI system is closely integrated with a tangible physical product that is placed on the NI market.

"It would not affect an NI business simply because it uses online or downloadable AI tools to manage work, analyse data, or carry out business functions.

"It would also not place obligations on the developers of those tools for their use in NI, unless the AI is closely integrated into a physical product placed on the NI market."

Examples of products which will be covered by the EU laws include a smart speaker with a built-in AI voice assistant or a smart watch requiring a manufacturer's AI health monitoring app.

The main idea of the EU law is to regulate AI based on its capacity to cause harm to society. The higher the risk, the stricter the rules with some AI applications being banned.

The government's examples of some physical products which could be banned include "a connected toy embedding AI that encourages children to undertake increasingly risky activities in exchange for reward or praise" or "an AI-connected camera with voice recognition that detects employee emotions ."

In general terms when the EU's rules on the regulation of goods are updated the UK government has to agree which of them should apply in NI.

In some circumstances the NI Assembly also has a vote on the matter.

articles.title: ChatGPT will now make you animated GIFs
articles.summary: OpenAI is rolling out an update for ChatGPT that will allow you to create and edit GIFs with the AI chatbot.
articles.body: ChatGPT can now create GIFs using a prompt or a photo uploaded to the AI chatbot. The update, which is rolling out alongside OpenAI’s new Images 2.6 model, allows you to adjust the GIF’s animation speed, edit individual frames, and share it with others. Before this change, ChatGPT couldn’t natively generate GIFs in a single step. An example shared by the company shows how ChatGPT can generate a GIF in response to the prompt, “can you make a gif of a cat dancing?” while also providing you with the option to change the playback speed and view it frame by frame. [Image: You can adjust speed and edit frames directly in ChatGPT. Along with support for GIF-making, the Images 2.6 update also enables faster image generation in ChatGPT, OpenAI says. The company says users now generate over 4 billion images per week across ChatGPT and its API, a jump from the 3 billion per week it reported in September. Images 2.6 is rolling out to all ChatGPT and Codex users across web, desktop, and mobile apps. OpenAI is also launching GPT-Image-2.6 Flare and Sunburst in its API for faster and higher-quality image generation.

articles.title: Nothing teases a screen-free AI device ahead of launch next month
articles.summary: Nothing CEO Carl Pei announced on X that it’s launching a new AI device next month, hinting at a screen-free design.
articles.body: Nothing CEO Carl Pei said in a post on X that the company’s launching its first AI device in December. That’s just a little over a year after Pei announced plans for “AI-native” devices and an AI operating system. He didn’t give away much about what exactly the new device is, only that one feature it won’t have is a screen: > “Our first AI-native product ships next month. It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.” Pei shared an image with the post that says “NOTHING(R)” in the top left corner, above an ambiguous black rounded corner. Last month, a rumor claimed Nothing is planning to launch two pairs of AI smart glasses, including one without cameras, and an earlier rumor said it’s “repositioning itself as an AI-first company” with a shift to AI accessories. [Image: Nothing’s AI device wouldn’t be the first screen-free AI gadget, following the likes of the Humane AI pin, the Friend, and even AI stuffed animals. OpenAI is also reportedly working on an AI smart speaker with Jony Ive. Pei alluded to earlier AI devices, saying, “the whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life.” He added, “Looking for the iPhone of AI today is a dead end.”

articles.summary:

> The lawsuit, ​filed on Tuesday in federal court in San Francisco ​by law firms Hausfeld and Gibbs Mura, alleges Axon ⁠has failed to comply with a California privacy provision by ​not disclosing how it collects, uses and shares plate data gathered ​through its camera systems. “Axon has created a mass-surveillance infrastructure that is practically impossible to avoid,” the lawsuit said.

articles.title: Anthropic tweaks how Claude Code handles requests about making games.
articles.summary:
After clamping down on AI video game clones amid the bigger influx of reverse-engineered games, the company is adjusting its approach to try and discourage straight-up copies:
> We’d added a short rule to the Opus 5.5 prompt to steer Claude away from recreating specific existing games, but it was also kicking in when you referenced one just to describe the mechanics you wanted.
> We’ve updated that rule in 2.1.317. You can name a game to describe what you want and Claude should now build an original game in that genre. If you ask for a copy of the original, it’ll offer to build something similar instead.

articles.title: DuckDuckGo pitches itself to schools amid backlash over Google's AI policy | TechCrunch
articles.summary: DuckDuckGo is courting schools frustrated by Google's AI restrictions, pointing educators to its search engine and options to disable AI features.
articles.body:
DuckDuckGo is pitching itself to schools after Google created an opening for the alternative search engine. On Tuesday, Google told schools they could turn off Gemini , but it said shutting off its other AI features would cost schools Google Search , as well.

DuckDuckGo, a company that focuses on user privacy by limiting data collection, clearly sees this as a moment to make inroads in education, where Google has historically dominated. According to figures Google has published in previous years, there are around 50 million Chromebooks in schools, used by students and educators, and its Google Classroom platform serves over 150 million users globally.

On X , DuckDuckGo’s founder and CEO, Gabriel Weinberg, pointed to the company’s online documentation , explaining how schools can switch their default search engine to DuckDuckGo’s service instead, adding, “get in touch for help.”

Meanwhile, DuckDuckGo’s chief public affairs officer, Kamyl Bazbaz, issued a stronger statement, writing , “Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless. Prove Google wrong.”

In an email to TechCrunch, DuckDuckGo chastised Google for its decision, adding that Google could easily turn off Search’s AI features for schools if it wanted to.

The company’s comments come as the American public is weighing how much AI they want to allow into their lives. As Tuesday night’s elections indicate, they don’t want AI data centers built in their towns. But using AI at work and school has become a common practice and requires a more nuanced discussion.

Knowing that educators have struggled with AI, Google developed technology called “ Guided Learning ” that is meant to help kids learn by walking through problem-solving steps rather than just providing them with an answer. But educators are still asking for tools that let them remove AI from the learning process altogether.

After the backlash on Tuesday, Google defended its decision, saying it was just responding to schools’ feedback. It said that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search would be off by default, and schools could choose to enable them individually.

The problem, of course, is that Google Search now heavily uses AI, through AI Overviews and a conversational AI Mode that answers users’ queries.

DuckDuckGo isn’t anti-AI, to be clear — it offers its own set of AI features, including a chat interface called Duck.ai and an AI search assistant.

However, unlike Google, it provides options to disable these features in both its search and browser settings, the company says. It also offers a dedicated website, noai.duckduckgo.com , where AI-assisted answers, AI-generated images, and AI feature suggestions are all turned off.

That flexibility may be driving demand for its services, as the company reported earlier this year that its app installs were up 30% as users rejected being force-fed Google’s AI Search.

articles.title: Apple Cuts Internal AI Usage Budgets in Move to Reduce Spending
articles.summary: Apple Inc. is reducing employee budgets for artificial intelligence usage as part of a cost-cutting effort, even as the company seeks to put AI at the center...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Apple Inc. is reducing employee budgets for artificial intelligence usage as part of a cost-cutting effort, even as the company seeks to put AI at the center of its operations.

Last month, Apple quietly lowered the daily spending cap for some engineers using AI models to $200 from $300, according to people with knowledge of the change. The company is now planning further cuts for some engineering teams, potentially reducing their daily allowances to as little as $100, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private.

The changes underscore the balancing act Apple faces as it tries to rein in costs while encouraging employees to incorporate AI more deeply into their daily work. The company is pushing to modernize its engineering processes and other internal operations with AI, even as it places tighter restrictions on how much employees can spend using the technology.

Many groups outside of engineering already face a $100 daily cap, but Apple has considered reducing that limit to as little as $25 for some teams, the people said. Employees who require higher allowances to perform their jobs will be able to seek exemptions from senior leadership.

A spokesperson for Cupertino, California-based Apple declined to comment.

The budgets cover tokens, the units of text and other data processed by AI models when handling requests. AI providers typically charge based on the volume of tokens consumed, with more advanced models generally costing more. Complex tasks such as writing and debugging software code can consume large quantities of tokens.

The restrictions reflect a broader shift across the technology industry, where companies that initially encouraged widespread experimentation with AI are increasingly scrutinizing the costs. The challenge is determining how much spending can be eliminated without undermining the efficiency gains that prompted companies to embrace the technology in the first place.

Reactions to the changes internally have been mixed. Some employees say that few workers were using their full $300 daily allowances, making the previous limits unnecessarily generous. Others see the reductions as a sign of broader cost cutting, adding to concerns about potential layoffs.

articles.title: Gemini for Home now plugs into AT&T’s smart security system
articles.summary: AT&T’s Connected Life System is now compatible with Gemini for Home, enabling a bunch of AI features, including home event summaries and the ability to search your recorded video history.
articles.body: AT&T’s smart home security system now integrates with Gemini for Home. The company says its Connected Life system is the “first” home security product to integrate with Google Home Premium, enabling a bunch of Gemini-powered features that can summarize home events, search your video history, and more. With the update, Gemini for Home can provide detailed descriptions about events captured by your security cameras, such as who delivered a package and how many items they dropped off. You can also search recorded video footage using natural language questions, like “What dug up the yard last night?” or “Who let the dogs out?”, as well as review daily summaries of activity in and outside your home. These features are only available with AT&T’s professional $29.99 / month Connected Life monitoring plan. AT&T is also adding the ability to automatically arm or disarm your home based on your proximity to your home. AT&T launched its Connected Life system last December in partnership with Google and Abode. It’s now taking advantage of Google’s Gemini-powered Home APIs, which allow smart home brands and developers to build AI-powered features into their devices. ADT has also hinted at bringing Gemini for Home features into its security systems.

articles.title: Goldman, Apollo in Talks to Sell SpaceX’s $40 Billion AI Deal
articles.summary: Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Apollo Global Management Inc. are in talks with Wall Street investors to start selling portions of a roughly $40 billion chip fi...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Apollo Global Management Inc. are in talks with Wall Street investors to start selling portions of a roughly $40 billion chip financing deal for SpaceX, just as the AI boom braces for upheaval following a sweeping Democratic victory.

The two firms have begun approaching potential buyers for the multi-tranche financing, according to people familiar with the matter. The deal, structured to keep the debt off SpaceX's balance sheet, is the largest arrangement of its kind for GPUs on record, SpaceX has said.

In some cases, investors are being asked to purchase slices of as much as $500 million before the official syndication process starts, in an effort to swiftly close the transaction, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private information. Syndication is slated to start soon, according to the people.

Representatives for Apollo and Goldman declined to comment. A representative for SpaceX didn't respond to a request for comment.

Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence venture announced the financing in October, with investors agreeing to the package before it priced.

That exposed lenders to market risk during a volatile period. Investors have retreated from the AI trade, questioning whether revenues can ever justify the breathtaking spend — a sentiment that turned lenders against some of SpaceX's neocloud competitors, including CoreWeave Inc.

Those pressures intensified after the Democrats swept into power in Congress following midterm elections, riding a wave of voter concerns over higher living costs and the war in Iran.

Data centers too became a fierce electoral flashpoint, particularly in Texas, which flipped blue just months after freezing new project approvals.

As the political landscape shifted overnight, the market reacted sharply, sending shares of both SpaceX and Tesla Inc. lower. SpaceX's data centers are based in Memphis, Tennessee, and it's developing other sites in Mississippi.

Under the $40 billion deal — a win for Musk — a special purpose vehicle managed by Apollo-backed Atlas SP will buy Nvidia Corp. chips and issue the debt held by lenders, Bloomberg previously reported. By using this structure, SpaceX protects its corporate credit ratings.

articles.title: Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor
articles.summary: The startup allows software engineers to deploy teams of agents to work on various aspects of a project simultaneously.
articles.body:
Meta has acquired Conductor , an AI coding startup that allows users to spin up software projects by deploying multiple agents into parallel workspaces.

The news was originally reported by Axios, and Conductor shared news of its acquisition on its blog.

“I have big news: Conductor is joining Meta,” wrote the startup’s founder and CEO, Charlie Holtz, on Wednesday. “We have some big, crazy plans for the next interface,” he added, teasing that the company would have “something new” for customers to use by “early next year.”

On X, Holtz also noted that he was looking forward to working with Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, and Nat Friedman, head of product at the company’s Superintelligence Labs. “They’ve been on an absolute tear, and I’m convinced MSL has the highest talent density of all the labs,” he added.

Meta confirmed the acquisition to TechCrunch but wouldn’t comment further or provide additional details about the deal.

Conductor, founded in 2024, only launched its core product just last summer. The company’s agentic teams, which can be deployed in the cloud, locally, or via a user’s phone, are designed to help software engineers work on separate, compartmentalized parts of a project in concert. The agents that the platform deploys aren’t developed in-house but come from major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI.

Holtz said that, until early next year, Conductor’s core features would continue to work as they previously have. The exception is Conductor’s cloud service, which will shut down on November 20, after which the company will begin deleting user cloud data.

Meta, which previously lagged behind in AI services, has spent the last several months trying to catch up. In August, the company launched Muse Code , its own coding agent. Meanwhile, the company’s recently launched Muse agents are seeing significant adoption, with the company recently reporting that the service had surpassed 10 million users. The company has also made a number of AI-related acquisitions over the past year, including Moltbook , the viral agent platform that made headlines.

articles.title: OpenAI is already trying to shape the 2028 election | TechCrunch
articles.summary: OpenAI’s Chris Lehane wants AI to define the 2028 election, proposing a new social contract that could benefit Americans while also advancing the AI giant’s own business interests.
articles.body:
OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane thinks the 2028 presidential election could be a defining moment for AI. And he wants politicians to start developing policies that address Americans’ concerns about the technology, rather than simply paying lip service to anti-AI sentiment and the backlash against data centers .

In a new essay , Lehane compares AI’s potential to reshape the economy to President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, the 1930s set of federal programs and reforms enacted after industrialization and the Great Depression shattered the old economic order. He observes that Americans today feel similarly anxious about losing control over their economic futures and urges politicians to find a “compelling third path” that allows people to share in AI’s benefits. He lays out five policy priorities, spanning worker protections and education to AI safety and data center development.

The essay comes on the heels of a stunning Democratic victory in the midterm elections, in which Democrats flipped control of Congress amid widespread voter frustration over the cost of living. Kate Brennan, who leads AI and corporate power policy at the AI Now Institute, told TechCrunch that Lehane’s rhetoric marks a notable shift from OpenAI’s policy agenda last year, which focused on accelerating AI development, reducing regulatory barriers, and expanding infrastructure.

Unsurprisingly, many of Lehane’s proposals would encourage wider AI adoption and support the infrastructure expansion companies like OpenAI need to grow. The original New Deal established protections for workers and placed constraints on corporate power. It’s less clear how Lehane’s vision would hold AI companies accountable for the economic disruption their technology could create.

“Invoking a New Deal metaphor is to invoke state capacity to actually benefit the public,” Brennan said. “This is written by a private company that is trying to advocate for policies for its own benefit. It is ahistorical at best and harmful at worst.”

While AI wasn’t a dominant issue in the midterms, opposition to data centers emerged as a major bipartisan concern in several races in the midterms. And Lehane may be right that AI will become a bigger part of the conversation over the next two years.

Affordability is already shaping up as a key issue for the 2028 election as Americans grapple with inflation, tariffs, and the rising cost of living. AI could become an increasingly large part of that conversation as voters stress about data centers hiking up electricity bills, AI replacing their jobs, and technology’s economic gains flowing only to a handful of wealthy companies.

Lehane acknowledges many of these concerns, but he offers few concrete proposals to prevent AI’s gains from becoming concentrated. Instead, he largely pitches AI as a path to greater prosperity for Americans willing to embrace it.

Take his proposals for the tax code. He suggests incentives for workers to learn AI skills, easier capital access for entrepreneurs, and new approaches to employee ownership and profit-sharing. Those are not the same as binding requirements that would ensure workers share in AI-generated wealth or that companies pay the costs of displacing workers.

“I was struck by how much of this policy is for a future…that is already predicated on mass AI adoption and AI benefiting society, which we have yet to see,” Brennan said. “All of it is predicated on benefiting from AI’s upside.”

Brennan said it would make more sense to see things like a revised corporate tax rate or tax incentives for hiring human beings rather than automating jobs, as well as ways to keep companies from amassing outsize market power.

Lehane’s emphasis on expanding AI’s economic opportunities, rather than limiting potential harms, extends to data centers. He notes concerns about data centers while emphasizing the construction jobs and local tax revenue they could generate. He then warns that politicians who support a data center moratorium could jeopardize America’s lead over China, going so far as to compare that stance to the 2002 vote to authorize the Iraq war.

Lehane also makes child safety and education central to his proposed agenda, stressing the importance of age-appropriate protections and safeguards around AI companions for minors. He also warns against keeping AI out of classrooms , arguing that doing so could lead to inequality between wealthy students and “children in rural communities.” But the argument takes for granted that AI improves learning, a claim that remains unproven and one critics say deserves more examination than more funding or individualized attention from human teachers.

Lehane also calls for enforceable AI safety standards, independent evaluations, public oversight, and the ability to restrict AI systems or use a kill switch to shut them down — though recent studies show that OpenAI and other AI labs haven’t published comprehensive plans for what they would do if a model escaped human control.

Brennan called these stances “disingenuous,” pointing to OpenAI’s history of opposing legislation designed to impose such measures. In 2024, for example, OpenAI opposed California’s AI safety bill, SB 1047, which would have mandated catastrophic risk evaluations and shutdown capabilities. Last year, OpenAI also sought to limit state regulation , arguing that states could undermine American innovation. The company has more recently shifted some of those positions, backing several state safety laws and saying it would be open to independent evaluators embedded in the company.

Lehane also argues that people should maintain control over consequential decisions made using AI, rather than handing off judgment entirely to machines. But that raises the question of what human control really looks like in a society where humans are increasingly being required to use AI in education, work, healthcare, and government.

Throughout his essay, Lehane frames AI as a technology that could give Americans back their sense of agency and economic opportunity. But he ties average Americans’ “middle class” success to participation in an economy increasingly shaped by companies like OpenAI. Whether his policies will meaningfully redistribute power or subtly entrench it is less clear.

TechCrunch reached out to OpenAI for more specifics on Lehane’s proposals and the company’s stances, but it did not respond by the time of publication.

articles.title: Almost no one uses AI agents to book their Uber, company says | TechCrunch
articles.summary: During its busiest week last quarter, Uber said only four people booked a ride using an AI agent.
articles.body:
Very few people are using personal AI agents to order Ubers, apparently. On the transportation giant’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, the company said that only four rides were ordered through an AI agent during its busiest week in October: the week of Halloween.

While more people used an AI agent to order food through its delivery service, Uber Eats, the volume was still fairly small compared to the overall number of trips.

Uber’s chief financial officer, Balaji Krishnamurthy, told Wall Street analysts on the call that the company handled around 320 million trips and orders across Uber and Uber Eats during the week of Halloween, but only 500 Uber Eats orders were placed by an AI agent.

“It is very, very early and very limited traction that we are seeing so far,” said CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, referring to the low number of orders placed by AI agents. “Listen, we hope that there will be more traction.”

The surprisingly low numbers of AI-initiated transactions come amid growing hype for a new wave of AI agents that don’t just answer questions but also handle tasks on users’ behalf. There’s been an explosion of personal AI startups, including one of the buzziest, Instinct, which was founded last year and raised its most recent round of funding at a $10 billion valuation. Meta’s Muse also became the No. 1 app in Apple’s U.S. App Store last month, topping 10 million users, per Meta’s own reporting . The company said many were using it to shop and transact with businesses.

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and SpaceXAI (Grok) are also now offering their own AI agents, as are numerous smaller startups.

Still, early numbers from public companies indicate the agentic web still has a long way to go. DoorDash, for instance, said last week on its earnings call that it has only received a few hundred orders from AI agents so far, as most customers are still placing orders through the DoorDash app.

Uber is seeing the same behavior, it seems. Khosrowshahi pointed out that the average time to book a ride is only 50 seconds in the company’s app, and re-ordering a favorite food only takes 90 seconds. That suggests an AI agent isn’t necessarily saving anyone time.

Despite the low number of AI-driven transactions, Khosrowshahi seemed bullish on the idea of agents in general. “We think that is another opportunity to reach our platform. We think it will be a net positive in terms of demand on the ecosystem,” he said.

Right now, there are around eight major AI assistants on the market, Khosrowshahi noted, and he expects that number to grow to more than 10 in time.

“Every single AI system company is talking to us,” he added.

articles.title: Qualcomm is betting big on data centers as smartphone sales sink
articles.summary: Qualcomm expects data center chips will eventually account for 30% of its business.
articles.body: With smartphone sales tanking by around 20 percent compared to 2025, Qualcomm is looking to data centers to help boost its bottom line. During its Q4 2026 earnings call, the company laid out its plans to make a splash in the AI data center business, through partnerships with companies like Amazon and Meta announced earlier this year. The company expects that portion of its business to grow quickly, forecasting around $650 million in data center revenue during the first quarter of 2027. But it anticipates that will reach $5 billion by the end of 2027 and $15 billion by 2029. Considering the company’s total revenue for 2026 was $10.4 billion, that would constitute a significant share of its earnings. It confirmed during the call that it expects data centers to eventually account for around 30 percent of its business. That’s not quite as ambitious as AMD, which says that it expects over 80 percent of its revenue will eventually come from data centers. But it suggests there’s plenty of demand that needs to be filled and enough AI money to go around.

articles.title: AI PACs spent millions trying to shape Congress — here's how they fared | TechCrunch
articles.summary: AI industry PACs spent millions influencing the 2026 midterms, with mixed results. Political groups are already looking toward the next election cycle.
articles.body:
Political groups both supporting and opposing the AI industry spent millions of dollars trying to influence Tuesday’s midterm elections and shape the future of AI regulation. That spending produced mixed results, with some of the most heavily backed candidates losing their races.

On the industry side, two AI-focused political action committees (PACs) that raised and spent money to influence the elections — American Mission and Building the Future — collectively spent $4.8 million to back South Carolina Senate candidate Darline Graham, who lost. American Mission is the Republican spending arm of Leading the Future (LTF), a broader political group backed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and the VC firm Andreessen Horowitz.

American Mission also spent more than $500,000 apiece supporting Republican House candidates Aaron Flint in Montana and Laurie Buckhout in North Carolina, both of whom lost. LTF’s Democratic spending arm, Think Big, had better luck backing Florida Rep. Jared Moskowitz, who won reelection.

Groups advocating for stronger AI safeguards also saw mixed results. Public First, which is backed by Anthropic, supported several Republicans who lost through its affiliated PAC but had more success backing Democratic candidates. It also contributed $3 million to a PAC supporting California state Sen. Scott Wiener, who was leading his race at the time of publication.

Meanwhile, Guardrails Alliance , a group that has sought to make taking money from AI companies a political liability, spent more than $1 million apiece opposing two candidates who lost: California Rep. Jimmy Gomez and Montana’s Aaron Flint. It also spent $300,000 supporting Angela Gonzales-Torres, who defeated Gomez.

It’s difficult to separate the impact of AI-related spending from the broader Democratic wave that swept Tuesday’s elections. Elon Musk, who reportedly poured half a billion dollars into supporting Republicans in the midterms, also saw many of his candidates lose . Indeed, LTF also backed some candidates it believed were likely to win, only to see them lose to the Dems.

For LTF, though, the general election wasn’t the main focus. The group told TechCrunch ahead of Election Day that it thinks primaries (the contests that choose each party’s nominee) are a more effective use of its money, because spending there can build name recognition and help candidates set up AI policy agendas.

LTF spent $27.38 million in the primaries, including $8 million alone on opposing New York Assembly member Alex Bores , who lost his bid for Congress back in June. When deciding whether it’s worth jumping into a general election race, LTF assesses how competitive the race is, whether it thinks spending could make a difference, and whether it should keep its powder dry for future elections.

Charlie Blaettler, political director of Guardrails Alliance, had a different theory for why LTF spent comparatively little in the general election.

“They don’t want their money to become an issue in these elections,” he said. He pointed to the Michigan Senate primary election, in which a pro-Israel lobbying group called AIPAC spent close to $30 million backing Democratic candidate Haley Stevens against Abdul El-Sayed. Stevens conceded the primary to El-Sayed, who went on to win the Senate seat.

“AIPAC became the story in that race,” Blaettler said. “We know people hate AI billionaires. They hate the people running these companies. They’re very distrustful and disgusted by the political spending and lobbying that the tech industry does. If they spend in a competitive race, they would just become an enormous liability for their candidates.”

The main fight among AIPACs, whether they are pro-industry or pro-regulation, is whether Congress should establish a national AI framework that overrides state laws , or whether states will maintain their own ability to impose safeguards.

Neither side seems poised to back down. LTF, which favors a single national AI framework, told TechCrunch it plans to keep spending in the 2028 elections, while Guardrails Alliance says it wants to keep opposing candidates backed by the AI industry.

Blaettler said that while LTF’s ads rarely touch on AI, instead focusing on popular issues for each candidate, Guardrail Alliance’s ads are specifically about who is taking money from the AI industry.

“Our goal is to make AI money politically toxic,” Blaettler said.
